newsitem.title: UK: FCAST-Pilkington yr earnings seen fragile.
newsitem.headline: FCAST-Pilkington yr earnings seen fragile.

text.p: Pilkington Plc will repeat warnings that tough market conditions demand drastic cost-cutting when it reports year results on Thursday, but analysts said they also want to hear how it plans to lift profits.

"The trading environment is extremely difficult so it will be up to internal management changes to produce gains," said one analyst who was not anticipating a significant improvement in the earnings picture until 1999.
The glass-maker last month appointed Paolo Scaroni chief executive to speed up the rate of cost cutting after earlier warnings that poor conditions in Germany would hobble profits.

Pilkington is forecast to post year profits of 130-135 million stg, sharply below the 212 million reported the previous year, following a March statement that profit before tax and exceptional items would not dip below 130 million stg.

Overcapacity in the German market has dogged Pilkington and analysts were hopeful that Scaroni would be able to secure significant staffing cuts in this region, despite the difficulties often faced in winning German headcount reductions.
Other analysts said the reorganisation plans must be twinned with a strategy to maintain prices and protect profit margins -- an area in which it had let itself down in the past.

One said that Roger Leverton, who Scaroni replaced on May 21, had already taken significant amount of costs out of the business and it was up to Scaroni to stabilise margins, otherwise any cost-cutting gains would be squandered.

"Pilkington has been a weak player -- it has to be much stronger, which involves taking costs out very quickly, notably at mid-management level, and taking a much tougher line on prices," the analyst said.
Pilkington's operating margins over the past five years have averaged 4.3 percent since 1992, versus levels more than double that at its arch rival Compagnie de Saint Gobain SA.
"It's early days in this man's strategy, but I think that there has to be the threat that if people (lower and middle management) drop prices, they'll be penalised," he added.
Pilkington shares, currently trading at 117p, have lost over a pound in price since last September and the upside looks capped until firm signals that the corner had been turned.

"I think we may have seen the worst (of the share price decline), but you won't expect them to rise substantially before we've had a chance to gauge the impact of the new regime," said another analyst who saw this taking at least nine more months.
